# Results — Study 377 (Bid-Ask-Bounce)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The famous **short-horizon mean
reversion** — "stocks that fell yesterday bounce back today" — tested against Roll's (1984)
rival explanation: it is the **bid-ask bounce** in disguise. The offline core is the **Roll
model** (a true random-walk price plus a bid/ask coin-flip); the real-tape **proxy** is a
one-day cross-sectional reversal book on a 35-name small/mid-cap basket (where spreads, hence
the bounce, are widest), measured **gross and net** of a one-way half-spread. Offline core &
control are deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — a fixed 35-name small/mid-cap US basket (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-08-11 → 2026-06-18 (**5,246** trading days; **20.9** years) |
| Spread | **inferred** (Roll 1984 estimator) — yfinance has no bid/ask, so the effective spread is read back from the lag-1 autocovariance; named a **proxy** throughout |
| Reversal book | equal-weight, dollar-neutral, cross-sectional: long yesterday's losers / short yesterday's winners |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag; one-way cost = half-spread × daily turnover (book re-forms each day) |

> **Proxy caveat (named on the Signal axis).** yfinance serves adjusted *closes*, not the
> bid/ask quotes Roll's estimator was built for, so our "spread" is **inferred** from the
> return autocovariance, not observed. A fixed surviving-names basket also carries
> **survivorship** — which, for a reversal book, if anything makes the *gross* edge look
> **better** than it would on a live, churning small-cap universe. Neither caveat rescues the
> verdict: the gross edge dies to a spread far smaller than the one the data itself implies.

## The apparent reversion is real — and so is the bounce

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Avg per-name lag-1 autocorrelation (the "mean reversion") | **−0.065** |
| Roll-implied effective spread (round-trip) | **109 bps** |

Small-cap daily returns *are* negatively autocorrelated (−0.065): yesterday's move tends to
partly reverse. That is the headline reversal "signal." But Roll's estimator reads an effective
round-trip spread of **≈109 bps** out of the *same* autocovariance — exactly the magnitude that
would manufacture this much apparent reversion from a pure bid-ask bounce around an efficient
price. The two readings are not independent: in Roll's model **they are the same number wearing
two hats.**

## The reversal book — gross looks like alpha, net is the spread you crossed

1-day entry lag; one-way cost = half-spread × daily turnover. Block-bootstrap *p* on the mean
daily PnL.

| one-way half-spread | mean PnL / day | daily win-rate | ann. Sharpe | *t* | bootstrap *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0 bps (gross)** | **+5.02 bps** | **54.7%** | **+1.20** | **+5.47** | 0.000 |
| 5 bps | −2.22 bps | 47.5% | −0.53 | −2.42 | 0.014 |
| 10 bps | −9.46 bps | 41.2% | −2.26 | −10.31 | 0.000 |
| 20 bps | −23.93 bps | 29.7% | −5.72 | −26.08 | 0.000 |

Read it carefully. **Gross**, the book is a textbook winner: **+5.0 bps/day**, a **54.7%**
daily win-rate, **Sharpe 1.20** at **t = 5.5** — comfortably "significant." So the reversion
*is* statistically real on the tape. But it lives **entirely inside the spread**: charge a one-way
half-spread of just **5 bps** (a 10 bps round-trip — *cheaper* than almost any small-cap
quote, and ten times cheaper than the 109 bps the data itself implies) and the mean PnL goes
**negative**, win-rate drops below 50%, Sharpe turns to **−0.53**. The "edge" was the bounce.

## Break-even — the gross edge is ~16× too thin to pay the spread

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Gross mean PnL | +5.02 bps / day |
| Average one-way turnover | 1.45 (book re-forms daily) |
| **Break-even half-spread** | **3.47 bps** (round-trip **6.9 bps**) |
| Roll-implied actual round-trip spread | **109 bps** |
| Actual spread ÷ break-even spread | **≈ 16×** |

The book breaks even at a round-trip cost of **~7 bps**. The spread the data itself implies you
must cross is **109 bps** — about **16× wider**. There is no execution venue, no patience, no
sizing that closes a gap that large: the gross reversion *is* the bid-ask bounce, and harvesting
it means paying the spread that created it. This is the entire teardown.

## Synthetic control #1 — the bounce manufactures the illusion, on data we control

Roll's single-asset model: a **pure random-walk** true price (zero reversion) plus a fair-coin
bid/ask bounce of half-spread *s*/2. The observed lag-1 autocovariance must equal **−(s/2)²**,
and Roll's estimator must read the planted spread back:

| planted spread *s* | observed cov₁ | theory −(s/2)² | observed ac₁ | recovered *s* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.000 (no bounce) | +1.3e−06 | 0 | +0.009 | — (cov₁ ≥ 0) |
| 0.005 | −5.0e−06 | −6.3e−06 | −0.032 | 0.0045 |
| 0.010 | −2.4e−05 | −2.5e−05 | −0.120 | 0.0097 |
| 0.020 | −9.7e−05 | −1.0e−04 | −0.280 | 0.0197 |

With **no** bounce the true price shows **no** reversion (ac₁ ≈ 0). Add a bounce and the
observed series acquires exactly the negative autocovariance Roll predicts — pure illusion,
because the true price never reverted. The estimator recovers the planted spread to the third
decimal. The machinery is faithful.

## Synthetic control #2 — gross vs net separates "real edge" from "the bounce"

A synthetic **panel** of 30 Roll assets (round-trip spread 40 bps ⇒ 20 bps one-way half-spread),
running the *same* reversal book as the real tape. `edge = 0` is the **pure bounce**; a large
planted AR(1) reversion (`edge = −0.25`) is a **genuine** mean reversion the book *should* harvest:

| planted reversion | gross mean/day | gross *t* | net @ 20 bps half-spread | net *t* | net Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **edge = 0** (pure bounce) | +3.31 bps | +7.5 | **−25.13 bps** | −56.9 | **−14.27** |
| **edge = −0.25** (real reversion) | +39.58 bps | +89.0 | **+8.01 bps** | +18.0 | **+4.51** |

The lesson in one table. With **no real reversion**, the book still shows a positive **gross**
PnL (t = 7.5) — the bounce — but **net of the spread it is deeply negative**: there was never
anything to harvest. Only when we plant a **genuine** reversion does the book survive the spread
**net-positive** (Sharpe +4.5). The synthetic control proves the engine is honest *and* that a
gross-positive reversal book is, by itself, no evidence of edge — exactly the trap the real tape
falls into.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The one-day reversion is statistically real on the tape (gross Sharpe 1.20,
  *t* = 5.5, ac₁ = −0.065), so it is not noise. But Roll's estimator reads a **109 bps** effective
  spread out of the *same* autocovariance, and the synthetic control shows a pure bounce produces
  an identical gross signal with **zero** underlying reversion. The effect is real-as-a-statistic
  but **mechanically a microstructure artefact**, not a clean price-predictive edge — literature
  + a gross signal that the bounce fully explains ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL. (Survivorship in the fixed
  basket tilts the *gross* number **up**, never down.)
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The book breaks even at a **~7 bps** round-trip and the spread you'd
  actually cross is **~109 bps** — **16× too wide**. Net of even a 10 bps round-trip the edge is
  already gone (Sharpe −0.53). You cannot harvest a reversion that *is* the spread. No NAV-scale
  strategy exists here.
- **Free lunch? — BUSTED.** "Buy yesterday's losers" backtests like alpha (Sharpe 1.2 gross)
  precisely because the backtest prints at mid/close and never pays the bounce it is trading
  against. Roll (1984) named the trap 40 years ago: short-horizon "mean reversion" is, in large
  part, **the bid-ask bounce in disguise.**
